quiz.why: Positive pressure reduces the work the failing heart must perform, so pressure falls as the patient improves. Read with the falling respiratory rate and rising saturation, this is response, and fluid would worsen the pulmonary edema.

quiz.q: A 32-week pregnant patient involved in a collision has BP 118/70 and HR 104. What should you conclude?
choices: Nothing reassuring; she can lose 1,500–2,000 mL before her pressure falls, and fetal distress can come first
She is hemodynamically stable and low priority
Her heart rate is abnormally low for pregnancy
Her blood pressure is abnormally high for 32 weeks
quiz.why: The 30%–50% volume expansion of pregnancy is a reserve, and uterine perfusion is sacrificed before maternal pressure changes. A heart rate of 104 is within the expected 10–20 bpm rise, and the pressure is unremarkable, which is precisely the trap.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old at 33 weeks has a blood pressure of 148/96, a headache and right upper quadrant pain. How should this be handled?
choices: As normal, since pregnancy raises blood pressure late in gestation
As a reading that requires no action because it is under 160/110
As gestational hypertension with symptoms concerning for preeclampsia, requiring urgent evaluation
As a measurement error, since pregnancy lowers blood pressure
quiz.why: After 20 weeks, 140/90 or higher defines gestational hypertension, and headache with right upper quadrant pain raises concern for preeclampsia. The 160/110 threshold defines severe range, not the point at which concern begins.

quiz.q: A collegiate distance runner has a resting heart rate of 42 and a blood pressure of 98/58. How should this be interpreted?
choices: As expected for a conditioned athlete, whose large stroke volume maintains output at a low rate
As symptomatic bradycardia requiring atropine
As evidence of a conduction block requiring pacing
As hypovolemia requiring fluid
quiz.why: Endurance training enlarges the ventricle and raises stroke volume, so the same cardiac output is produced at 40–60 beats per minute with a low resting pressure. Treatment is indicated by symptoms, not by a number outside a population range.

quiz.q: A football player collapses during a summer practice with a rectal temperature of 41.2 C and confusion. What is the priority?
choices: Give an antipyretic and transport
Obtain a full set of vitals before any cooling
Begin aggressive cooling immediately, ideally cold-water immersion, before transport
Warm the patient to prevent shivering during transport
quiz.why: Core temperature above 40 C with altered mental status is exertional heat stroke, and current practice is cool first, transport second, because outcome tracks time above the critical temperature. Antipyretics do nothing, since the set point never moved.

quiz.q: A ward patient has RR 24, SpO2 93% on 4 L, BP 98/58, HR 118, temperature 38.4 C and is newly confused. Which statement best applies?
choices: The values individually are borderline, so monitoring can continue
The aggregate early warning score is high and several parameters independently meet rapid response criteria, so escalate now
Only the temperature needs treatment
The supplemental oxygen makes the saturation reassuring
quiz.why: Multiple parameters are abnormal simultaneously, which is exactly what aggregate scores such as NEWS2 are built to detect, and new confusion is itself a standalone rapid response trigger. Supplemental oxygen makes a 93% saturation more concerning, not less.

quiz.q: You have twice reported a systolic of 84 and been told to chart it and wait. What should you do next?
choices: Continue monitoring, since the concern has been reported twice
Chart that the concern was dismissed and take no further action
Repeat the pressure a third time and wait for a change
Apply the two-challenge rule, state that this is a safety issue, and activate the rapid response team
quiz.why: The two-challenge rule says that after raising a concern twice without it being addressed, you escalate up the chain, and CUS language provides the wording. Most rapid response policies also list staff concern as a standalone activation criterion.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 8-month-old, breathing fast and not feeding
scenarios.intro: Dispatch: 8-month-old, difficulty breathing. Mother reports three days of cough and runny nose, worse overnight. The baby has taken only a few ounces since yesterday and has had two wet diapers in 24 hours. It is February.

steps.prompt:
You are still in the doorway. The baby is in her mother's arms, awake, with a soft grunt at the end of each breath. You can see her ribs pulling in with every effort. Her lips are pink; her hands look mottled.

What do you do in the first ten seconds?

choices.text: Run the Pediatric Assessment Triangle from across the room: appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
choices.feedback: Correct. You already have two abnormal sides before touching her: grunting and retractions on work of breathing, and mottling on circulation. That is a sick infant, established in seconds and without equipment.

choices.text: Take the baby from the mother and start a hands-on assessment immediately
choices.feedback: Premature. Handling changes everything you were about to measure, especially respiratory rate and effort, and separating an infant from a parent raises distress. Look first.

choices.text: Attach a pulse oximeter and wait for a number before forming an impression
choices.feedback: Too narrow. A cold, mottled infant is exactly the patient whose oximeter reading will be weak or absent, and the visual findings you already have outrank a number you may not get.

choices.text: Ask the mother for the full history before observing the baby
choices.feedback: The history matters and it can wait ten seconds. Observing before the room changes is a one-time opportunity; the history is still available afterward.

steps.prompt:
You count for a full minute with the chest exposed. Respirations `66`, with nasal flaring and subcostal retractions. Heart rate `172`. Capillary refill `4` seconds at the sternum. She looks at you but does not reach out.

Your partner says the rate is high but her age band goes up to `50`, so it is not that far off. What do you say?

choices.text: A sustained rate over 60 in an infant is abnormal at any age band, and combined with grunting, flaring, retractions and a 4-second refill this is severe distress
choices.feedback: Right. Grunting alone is always significant, and the combination here describes an infant working at maximum with failing peripheral perfusion. The band ceiling is a range, not a target.

choices.text: Agree that 66 is close enough to the upper limit to be reassuring
choices.feedback: Wrong, and dangerously so. The upper end of a range describes well infants at rest, not a sustained rate with grunting and retractions. This baby is above the band and working hard to stay there.

choices.text: Note the temperature of 38.2 C and attribute the whole picture to fever
choices.feedback: Fever does raise heart and respiratory rate, roughly 8–10 bpm per degree, but it does not produce grunting, flaring, retractions or a 4-second capillary refill. Those are work and perfusion findings.

choices.text: Focus on the SpO2 of 91% as the only number that matters
choices.feedback: It matters and it is not alone. In an infant, work of breathing and perfusion findings carry more information than saturation, which can hold up until quite late.

steps.prompt:
En route, with blow-by oxygen and the child upright on her mother's lap, you recheck.

Respirations `48`, heart rate `150`, `SpO2 94%`, and she is now fussing loudly and pushing the mask away.

choices.text: Genuine improvement: rate and heart rate down, saturation up, and she has the energy to protest
choices.feedback: Correct, and the protest is the best part. A child who fights you has appearance, which is the most sensitive element of the triangle. This is what real improvement looks like.

choices.text: Concerning: the falling respiratory rate suggests exhaustion
choices.feedback: That is the right worry applied to the wrong case. Exhaustion comes with a falling saturation, decreasing responsiveness, and a quieter chest. Here the saturation rose and she became more interactive, not less.

choices.text: Remove the oxygen since the saturation is now 94%
choices.feedback: Premature. She reached 94% on oxygen while still working hard. Removing support because the supported number looks acceptable is exactly the error early warning scores are built to catch.

choices.text: No conclusion is possible without a blood pressure
choices.feedback: A blood pressure would add little here and is often omitted under age 3 by protocol. Heart rate, work of breathing, skin and appearance have already made the assessment.

steps.prompt:
You give report at the pediatric bay. The nurse has seen twenty respiratory infants today and is half-listening.

What do you lead with?

choices.text: Eight months, grunting and retracting on arrival, RR 66 and HR 172 with 4-second refill and 91% on room air; now RR 48, HR 150, 94% on blow-by; two wet diapers in 24 hours
choices.feedback: This is the report. Two timed sets showing direction, the work-of-breathing findings that made her sick, the perfusion finding, and the feeding and diaper history that quantifies the dehydration.

choices.text: Eight-month-old with a cold, currently satting 94%
choices.feedback: This buries the case. A single supported saturation with no work-of-breathing findings and no trend makes a severely distressed infant sound like the twenty before her.

choices.text: Lead with the temperature of 38.2 C and the three-day history
choices.feedback: Accurate but poorly prioritized. The fever is the least discriminating fact you have; the grunting, the refill and the trend are what separate this baby from the others.

choices.text: Hand over the run sheet and let the nurse read the numbers
choices.feedback: Insufficient in a busy bay. A verbal trend with the direction stated out loud is what gets a patient seen sooner, which is the entire purpose of the handoff.

scenarios.debrief:
Almost everything that mattered here was available before anyone touched the baby. Grunting, flaring, retractions and mottling are the Pediatric Assessment Triangle, and they had already established severe distress while the numbers were still being counted.

Two numeric points carry forward. A sustained respiratory rate over 60 in an infant is abnormal at any age band, and the ceiling of a published range describes well infants at rest rather than a target to aim at. And a full 60-second count with the chest exposed, taken before handling, is the only way to get a usable pediatric respiratory rate.

The improvement check is the subtle part. A falling respiratory rate is alarming in a tiring asthmatic and reassuring here, and the difference was the rest of the picture: the saturation rose and the child became more interactive, not less. The direction of a number only means something inside the story.

Finally, the handoff. Two timed sets and the work-of-breathing findings are what made this infant visible in a bay full of respiratory infants.

scenarios.title: Triage: 31F at 34 weeks, headache since this morning
scenarios.intro: A 31-year-old at 34 weeks of pregnancy walks up to triage with her partner. She has had a headache since waking, says it will not go away with acetaminophen, and mentions her hands and face look puffy. She apologizes for coming in over a headache.

steps.prompt:
You take an automatic pressure over her sleeve while she is talking, with her arm resting in her lap below heart level. It reads `138/86`. Heart rate `96`.

Your colleague says that is basically normal. What do you do?

choices.text: Repeat it manually on a bare arm supported at heart level with her quiet, because cuff over clothing, a dependent arm and talking all read falsely high or low
choices.feedback: Correct, and it cuts both ways here. Those errors usually push a reading up, so the true value could be lower, but the measurement as taken is not trustworthy enough to clear or condemn her. Get a real number.

choices.text: Accept 138/86 and route her to the waiting room as low acuity
choices.feedback: Two problems. The measurement technique was invalid, and 138/86 in a 34-week pregnant patient with headache and edema is already close to the gestational hypertension threshold of 140/90.

choices.text: Accept the reading but flag it because pregnancy lowers blood pressure, so 138/86 is relatively high
choices.feedback: Good reasoning about pregnancy physiology, and still built on an untrustworthy number. The instinct is right; the measurement needs repeating before it carries any weight.

choices.text: Skip the pressure and go straight to fetal monitoring
choices.feedback: Fetal assessment will happen and it does not replace a maternal blood pressure. In a patient with headache and edema at 34 weeks, that number is the one that classifies her.

steps.prompt:
Repeated correctly: `156/98`, confirmed twice, four minutes apart, both arms within `4 mmHg`.

She now mentions that her vision has been going spotty since lunch and that her upper abdomen aches on the right.

choices.text: Recognize gestational hypertension with headache, visual change and right upper quadrant pain: concerning for preeclampsia, and escalate immediately
choices.feedback: Correct. After 20 weeks, 140/90 or higher is gestational hypertension, and this symptom triad moves the concern to preeclampsia. This is an immediate escalation, not a queue position.

choices.text: Note that 156/98 is below the severe threshold of 160/110, so she can wait in the queue
choices.feedback: This is the trap. The 160/110 line defines severe range; it is not the point at which concern begins. With headache, visual change and epigastric pain, she is already a high-acuity patient.

choices.text: Attribute the visual spots to the headache and the abdominal ache to the pregnancy itself
choices.feedback: Both explanations are individually plausible and together they form a recognized pattern. Explaining away each symptom separately is how this diagnosis gets missed.

choices.text: Recheck the pressure a third time before doing anything
choices.feedback: You already have two confirmed readings four minutes apart in both arms. Further rechecking is delay disguised as diligence.

steps.prompt:
The charge nurse is on the phone. The physician is in a room. You have about twenty seconds when someone looks up.

How do you say it?

choices.text: Thirty-one-year-old at 34 weeks, 156/98 confirmed manually twice, with headache, visual changes and right upper quadrant pain. I am concerned about preeclampsia. I need her seen now, not in the queue.
choices.feedback: Complete SBAR with the one element people drop: a specific ask with a timeframe. Situation, background, assessment, recommendation, said in under twenty seconds.

choices.text: There is a pregnant patient in triage with a high blood pressure whenever someone gets a chance
choices.feedback: No ask, no timeframe, no assessment. This is the report that gets acknowledged and then sits, which is exactly the escalation failure that precedes most deterioration events.

choices.text: Chart the vitals and the symptoms thoroughly and let the record speak
choices.feedback: The chart is a record, not a person. A dangerous number that lives only in the chart has not been communicated to anyone who can act on it.

choices.text: Give only the blood pressure, since it is the most objective finding
choices.feedback: Incomplete. 156/98 alone sounds ordinary. It is the combination with headache, visual change and right upper quadrant pain that makes this urgent, and that combination has to be said out loud.

steps.prompt:
She is taken back. You are asked to put her on the monitor and take a repeat set.

You have to lay her flat briefly for an abdominal examination. Within a minute she goes pale and says she feels like she is going to pass out.

choices.text: Roll her onto her left side or manually displace the uterus to the left, because after 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when supine
choices.feedback: Correct, and it works within seconds. Supine hypotensive syndrome is mechanical: relieve the compression and venous return, cardiac output and pressure all recover.

choices.text: Treat the drop as evidence that the earlier hypertension reading was wrong
choices.feedback: No. Two different mechanisms are in play. Her baseline pressure is elevated, and this acute fall is positional caval compression. Both findings are real.

choices.text: Give a fluid bolus while keeping her flat
choices.feedback: Harmful ordering. The problem is mechanical obstruction of venous return, not volume. Leaving her flat sustains the compression, and volume loading a possible preeclamptic patient is not a benign default.

choices.text: Sit her fully upright to relieve the pressure
choices.feedback: Better than flat, and not the standard answer. Left lateral positioning or manual left uterine displacement directly unloads the vena cava and is what protocols specify.

scenarios.debrief:
Three distinct skills carried this case, and the patient nearly slipped through on each one.

The measurement. A cuff over clothing, on a dependent arm, in a talking patient, produced a plausible number that was nearly 20 mmHg off. Nothing flagged it. Technique errors never announce themselves, which is why repeating a management-changing reading manually is a habit rather than a decision.

The threshold. After 20 weeks, 140/90 is gestational hypertension and 160/110 is severe. Reading 156/98 as safe because it sits below the severe line inverts what those numbers mean, and headache, visual change and right upper quadrant pain complete a pattern that should be recognized as a unit rather than explained away symptom by symptom.

The escalation. The SBAR ended with a specific ask and a timeframe, which is the element most often left off and the reason concerns get acknowledged and then wait.

The last step is a reminder that pregnancy physiology keeps producing new mechanisms. Her chronic problem was hypertension; her acute problem sixty seconds later was mechanical caval compression from lying flat, fixed in seconds by left lateral positioning.
